audience: Curious general viewers, including interested teens and beginner programmers
subject: computer-science
question: Why can checking one billion items for duplicates take about 79 years or 10 seconds in an illustrative operation model?
payoff: Comparing every unordered pair grows quadratically; scanning with a set uses two modeled operations per item when there are no duplicates, subject to average-case hash behavior.

claims.text: At 1,000 distinct items, duplicate detection compares 499,500 unordered pairs.
assumptions: No duplicate exists, so the algorithm runs to completion.
Each unordered pair is compared once.
limitations: Counts abstract operations; operations have unequal real costs.

claims.text: At 1,000 distinct items, the set scan models 2,000 membership and insertion operations.
assumptions: No duplicate exists, so the algorithm runs to completion.
Model one set membership test and one set insertion for each item.
limitations: Counts abstract operations; operations have unequal real costs.

claims.text: Python set membership is O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case; set insertion is typically O(1) amortized under suitable hashing.
assumptions: Hashes distribute values well enough that collisions are uncommon.
Set insertion has similar average behavior to dict insertion, as the wiki describes their implementations as similar.
limitations: Worst-case set membership is O(n); a set uses extra memory and actual insertion and membership costs differ from pair comparisons.

beats.narration: A thousand items. Check every pair for duplicates: nearly half a million comparisons. Or scan with a set: two thousand lookups and insertions.
beats.onScreen: No duplicates: 499,500 pairs vs 2,000 set operations

beats.narration: Ten times the items. Pair checks grow about a hundredfold. The set scan grows tenfold.
That growth is time complexity. Pair checks grow like n squared; a set scan grows like n, on average.
beats.onScreen: Time complexity: O(n²) pairs vs average O(n) set scan

beats.narration: Imagine two hundred million abstract operations per second, equally fast. With no duplicates, one million items: about forty-two minutes versus ten milliseconds. One billion: about seventy-nine years versus ten seconds.
beats.onScreen: Illustrative model: 1 billion distinct items, ~79 years vs 10 seconds

beats.narration: Same task: prove there are no duplicates. The nested loop compares every distinct pair. The set checks and stores each item once. Hash lookups are constant time on average, not guaranteed.
beats.onScreen: No duplicates: n(n-1)/2 comparisons vs 2n set operations

beats.narration: Same answer. In this hypothetical model, seventy-nine years becomes ten seconds. Which method would you choose?
